title: Transactional Funding for Double Closings Explained: A Complete Guide for Real Estate Wholesalers
excerpt: Transactional funding makes double closings possible without using your own cash, letting wholesalers flip contracts same-day. Learn exactly how it works, what it costs, and how to use it to close more deals.

sections.content: If you've been wholesaling real estate for any length of time, you've probably heard about double closings. They let you buy a property from a motivated seller and immediately sell it to your end buyer — all on the same day. The problem? You still technically need to fund the first purchase, even if only for a few hours. That's exactly where transactional funding comes in. Understanding transactional funding for double closings is one of the most valuable things any wholesaler can learn, and this guide breaks it all down in plain English.
What Is a Double Closing?

A double closing — also called a back-to-back closing — involves two separate real estate transactions that happen on the same day or within a very short window. In the first transaction (the A-to-B closing), you buy the property from the seller. In the second transaction (the B-to-C closing), you immediately sell that same property to your end buyer. You briefly hold title to the property between the two closings, which is what makes it a true double closing rather than a simple assignment of contract.

Double closings are especially useful when you don't want to disclose your profit margin to either the seller or the buyer. With a simple assignment, your fee shows up clearly on the closing documents. With a double closing, your spread stays private. This makes double closings the preferred method in many competitive wholesale markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), where deals move fast and margins can be substantial.
What Is Transactional Funding?

Transactional funding is a very short-term loan — sometimes called flash funding or same-day funding — designed specifically to fund the A-to-B leg of a double closing. Unlike traditional hard money loans or bank financing, transactional funding is meant to be repaid within hours or days, not months. The lender provides the capital you need to close with the seller, and once your end buyer funds the B-to-C closing, those proceeds pay back the transactional lender immediately.
Transactional funding is essentially a bridge that lets you stand in the middle of a deal with nothing but a contract and a buyer — and still walk away with a check at the end of the day.
How Transactional Funding Works: Step by Step
The mechanics are straightforward once you see them laid out. Here's a typical double closing timeline using transactional funding:

items: Step 1 — You get a property under contract with a motivated seller at a below-market price. Let's say you lock it up for $120,000.
Step 2 — You find an end buyer willing to purchase the property at $145,000, giving you a $25,000 gross spread.
Step 3 — You apply for transactional funding to cover the $120,000 purchase price plus closing costs on the A-to-B transaction.
Step 4 — On closing day, the transactional lender wires funds directly to the title company to close your purchase from the seller.
Step 5 — Within hours (sometimes the same afternoon), the B-to-C closing happens. Your end buyer funds $145,000 to the title company.
Step 6 — The title company pays back the transactional lender from the B-to-C proceeds, then cuts you a check for your profit minus fees.
Step 7 — The entire cycle is complete. You never used a dollar of your own money, and you walk away with your spread.

sections.content: Always confirm your end buyer has their financing locked in before scheduling the double closing. Transactional lenders charge daily fees, and a delayed B-to-C closing can eat into your profit fast. Some lenders charge 1-2% for 24 hours with additional daily rates after that.
What Does Transactional Funding Cost?

Transactional funding is intentionally expensive on a percentage basis — but remember, you're only paying for a matter of hours or days. Most transactional lenders charge between 1% and 2.5% of the loan amount for a one- to two-day funding window, with additional fees for each day the loan remains open. On a $120,000 loan at 2%, you'd pay $2,400 in funding fees. Compared to your $25,000 gross spread, that leaves you with a healthy net profit of around $22,600 before closing costs.

Some lenders also charge a flat origination fee ranging from $500 to $1,500, plus any wire fees. Always ask for a full fee schedule before committing. Who Provides Transactional Funding?
Private Transactional Lenders

The majority of transactional funding comes from private lenders who specialize exclusively in this type of short-term deal financing. They are not banks. They don't pull your credit, require income verification, or demand an appraisal. Their approval is based almost entirely on one thing: do you have a verified end buyer with funding already in place? Most private transactional lenders can approve and fund a deal within 24 to 48 hours of receiving your documentation.
Hard Money Lenders

Some hard money lenders also offer transactional funding as a side product. The approval process may be slightly more involved than a pure transactional lender, but they can sometimes offer better rates if you have an established relationship. If you're flipping properties in active markets and already working with a hard money lender, ask them directly whether they offer same-day or 24-hour bridge funding for double closings.
What You Need to Qualify
Qualifying for transactional funding is far simpler than any traditional loan. Most lenders require the following:

items: A signed purchase contract between you (the wholesaler) and the seller (A-to-B contract)
A signed purchase contract between you and your end buyer (B-to-C contract)
Proof of your end buyer's funds or financing — a bank statement, proof of funds letter, or lender commitment letter
Title company or closing attorney contact information
A basic one-page application with your LLC or entity information

sections.content: Notice what's NOT on that list: your credit score, tax returns, income documentation, or property appraisal. The deal itself is the collateral. If the spread makes sense and your buyer has real money, you'll almost always get approved.
Common Mistakes to Avoid

items: Not confirming your title company handles double closings — some won't, so always ask upfront
Failing to verify your end buyer's funds before ordering transactional funding — a phantom buyer will cost you fees with no closing
Forgetting to factor both sets of closing costs into your profit calculation
Using transactional funding on thin deals where the fees eliminate your margin
Not having a backup transactional lender — if your primary falls through, you need options fast

sections.content: Build relationships with two or three transactional lenders before you need them. When a deal is closing in 48 hours, you don't have time to shop around. Vet your lenders, understand their fee structures, and have them pre-approve your entity so you can move quickly when a deal hits.
Is Transactional Funding Right for Your Deals?

Transactional funding makes the most sense when your spread is large enough to absorb the fees and still leave a meaningful profit. As a general rule, most experienced wholesalers avoid using transactional funding on deals with less than a $10,000 to $15,000 gross spread. Below that threshold, the funding fees and double closing costs can shrink your take-home to almost nothing. On larger deals — $30,000, $50,000, or more in equity — transactional funding is an extremely efficient tool.

Double closings with transactional funding are also a smart move any time you want to keep your profit private, protect a sensitive seller relationship, or handle a situation where your end buyer's lender won't allow a simple assignment. In competitive wholesale markets where deals move fast and buyers are sophisticated, having this tool in your toolkit separates serious operators from beginners.
